rules.title: Daily price limit
points: A stock can rise or fall at most 15% from the previous close in one day. This replaced the old 10% limit from 20 April 2026.
The pre-open session (10:30 to 10:45) allows 5% (it was 2%).
A stock locked at its limit with buyers waiting means strong demand; locked at the lower limit means sellers cannot find buyers. Both can reverse quickly.
rules.note: Source: NEPSE rule change reported 17 to 20 April 2026.

rules.title: Market-wide trading halt
points: If the NEPSE index moves 5% during the first two hours of trading, trading stops for 15 minutes.
If the index moves 8%, trading is suspended for the rest of the day.
This replaced the old three-step system of 4%, 5% and 6%.
rules.note: Reports of the exact timing differ slightly; check the latest NEPSE notice.

rules.title: Trading days and hours
points: NEPSE trades Monday to Friday. Saturday and Sunday are closed, and so are public holidays.
Pre-open session: 10:30 to 10:45 (orders only, to set the opening price). Regular trading runs from 11:00 to 15:00.
Sanket updates live prices only while the market is open and stores the final numbers after the close.

rules.title: Buying, selling and settlement (T+2)
points: You need a demat account (BOID, with a Depository Participant), a MeroShare login and a trading account (TMS) with a broker.
Shares you buy reach your demat account two trading days later (T+2), and the money moves on the same cycle.
You cannot sell shares that have not yet arrived in your demat account, and shares you sell must be in it before the trade.
The face value of most shares is Rs 100. The smallest buy is 1 unit (kitta).

rules.title: Brokerage and other costs
points: Broker commission is a slab of the trade value: 0.40% (up to Rs 50,000), 0.37%, 0.34%, 0.30% and 0.27% for the largest trades, with a minimum of Rs 10 per trade.
SEBON fee: 0.015% of the trade value.
DP charge: Rs 25 per transaction, plus a yearly demat fee from your DP.
The Sanket Fee Calculator on the Goal page applies these for you.
rules.note: Check your broker and the current schedule; these slabs are what Sanket uses in its calculators.

rules.title: Capital gains tax (profit on selling)
points: Profit from selling shares is taxed for individuals: 7.5% if you held them for up to a year, 5% if you held them for more than a year.
The tax is taken on the profit only, after the buying price and costs. A loss is not taxed.
The broker collects it when you sell and it is added to your trade bill.
rules.note: Rates are what Sanket uses; confirm with the latest Finance Act.

rules.title: Dividend, bonus and tax on them
points: Cash dividend and bonus shares are declared as a % of the share's face value (Rs 100). A 10% cash dividend is Rs 10 per share.

Tax on dividend is 5% for individuals and is cut before you are paid. Bonus shares are taxed as well; the company handles it before the shares are issued, so check the notice for what you actually receive.
After a bonus, the price falls on the book-close adjustment day with no real loss; Sanket adjusts older prices so charts do not show a fake crash.
Dividend yield = yearly dividend per share ÷ price. Check it against the price you pay, not the face value.

rules.title: Book close and AGM
points: The company fixes a book-close date. Only shareholders on the register on that date get the dividend, bonus or right share.
Because of T+2 settlement, you must buy early enough for the shares to reach your demat account before that date. The company's notice gives the last day to buy.
On the first trading day after book close the price is adjusted for the dividend or bonus.
The AGM is the meeting where shareholders approve the dividend. See the Events calendar on the Market page.

rules.title: Promoter shares and public shares
points: Promoter shares belong to the founders and early investors. Public shares are the ones sold to ordinary investors in the IPO and traded daily.
Both have the same face value (Rs 100) and carry the same dividend, bonus, right and voting rights.
Promoter shares cannot be sold during the lock-in period, so only public shares are traded freely. When the lock-in ends, promoter shares can be sold like ordinary shares.
A big promoter holding means few shares in the market. When a lock-in ends, many shares can suddenly be for sale, which often pushes the price down.
The Company figures card on each stock page shows the promoter and public split when the data is available.

rules.title: Promoter lock-in (hydro and others)
points: Promoters cannot sell for 3 years after the shares are allotted to the general public in the IPO. The clock starts from that allotment.
This applies to sectors such as hydropower, investment companies, manufacturing and hotels. Banks and insurance companies are treated differently.
The Securities Board (SEBON) requires NEPSE, CDS and the company to announce the end of a lock-in 30 days before it happens.
Promoters who leave senior positions also face a one-year limit on selling.
Watch the date: the days before and after a large lock-in ends are often volatile. The Events calendar shows notices when they are published.
rules.note: Read the company's prospectus and the SEBON notice for the exact date and shares involved.

rules.title: Hydropower share structure
points: A hydropower company must offer between 15% and 49% of its capital to the public. Banks and financial institutions must offer at least 30%.
Up to 5% of the public issue can be reserved for local residents of the project area, depending on the business. Local shares have a 3-year lock-in, while general public shares can be traded at once.
A company can issue public shares while the project is still under construction, so the share price depends a lot on whether the plant is built on time.
Hydropower earnings depend on river flow and on the power purchase agreement, so quarterly results change with the seasons.
rules.note: Check each company's prospectus for its own split.

rules.title: Applying for an IPO
points: Apply through MeroShare: My ASBA, choose the issue, enter the units, your bank and your CRN, and your transaction PIN.
The minimum application is usually 10 units (Rs 1,000 at face value). The maximum depends on the issue.
The money is only blocked in your bank account (ASBA), not paid, until the allotment. If you are not allotted, it is released.
When more people apply than there are shares, allotment is by lottery. Applying more units does not raise your odds by much in a large issue, so apply what you can afford to hold.
An IPO sells at face value or a premium. After listing, the price is set by the market and can be far above or below the issue price.

rules.title: Right shares
points: A right share lets existing shareholders buy new shares at a set price (often face value), in a ratio such as 1:0.5, before the public can.
You must be on the register on the book-close date and then apply (through MeroShare) and pay within the issue period.
After the right issue the price falls to reflect the extra shares, so Sanket adjusts older prices.
You can sell your right entitlement or ignore it; if you ignore it, your holding is diluted.

rules.title: Auctions (promoter and unsold shares)
points: Some companies sell blocks of shares (for example promoter shares after the lock-in) through an auction instead of the normal market.
Bids are collected in a set window and the shares are allotted at the bid prices as the notice describes.
Auctions appear in the Events calendar on the Market page.

rules.title: Mutual funds and NAV
points: A mutual fund pools many investors' money and a fund manager invests it in shares and bonds.
NAV (net asset value) per unit is what one unit is worth on the books. Closed-end funds trade on NEPSE, often below or above their NAV.
Open-ended funds must publish their NAV every day under the new SEBON rules.
A unit trading well below NAV may look cheap, but check the fund's dividends and what it holds.

rules.title: EPS, P/E, P/B and book value
points: EPS (earnings per share) = profit ÷ number of shares. Higher is better if it keeps growing.
P/E = price ÷ EPS. It says how many years of the current profit you pay for. Compare only with similar companies in the same sector.
Book value = what each share would get if the company were closed and all its debts paid. P/B = price ÷ book value.
A low P/E is not always cheap: profit may be about to fall. A high P/E can be fair if profit is growing fast.
Quarterly figures are not a full year: the EPS reported for a quarter is for 3 months only (the figure may be annualised in some pages).

rules.title: Chart indicators in plain words
points: Moving average: the average closing price of the last 20, 50 or 200 days. Price above it means an uptrend.
RSI: 0 to 100. Above 70 the stock has risen fast (stretched up); below 30 it has fallen fast. Strong trends stay stretched for weeks.
MACD: compares a fast and a slow average. The line crossing above its signal line is a sign momentum is turning up.
Bollinger bands: a channel around the 20-day average. Touching the outer band shows a stretched move.
Support is a price where it stopped falling before; resistance is where it stopped rising. They are habits, not walls.

rules.title: Brokers, floorsheet and what they show
points: Every trade is listed in the floorsheet with the buying broker, the selling broker, the quantity and the rate. Broker numbers are published after the market closes.
A broker buying much more than it sells over several days may be building a position for one client or many; it is a clue, not proof.
The same broker on both sides of a trade (wash trade) adds volume without a change of owner, so heavy wash trading makes volume misleading.

rules.title: Staying safe: simple risk habits
points: Only invest money you will not need for years. Never borrow to buy shares.
Decide the most you can lose on one stock before buying, and size the position so that loss is small.
Spread your money over different sectors. One bad stock should not hurt much.
Be careful with rumours and tips, and with stocks that move to the limit on thin volume.
Past analysis is not a promise of future returns. Sanket gives analysis, not investment advice.

rules.title: Who does what: SEBON, NEPSE, CDSC
points: SEBON (Securities Board of Nepal) is the regulator. It approves IPOs and makes the rules.
NEPSE (Nepal Stock Exchange) runs the trading system and publishes prices.
CDS and Clearing (CDSC) keeps the demat accounts and runs MeroShare.
Brokers are licensed by SEBON. If you have a complaint, you can take it to the broker, then NEPSE or SEBON.
